item.title: These ARE the droids you’re looking for
item.description:
There’s an old leadership fantasy that goes something like this: The CISO surveys a sprawling technology estate, discovers 11 tools doing the work of four, calculates the licensing savings, selects a shiny new strategic platform and declares that consolidation has begun. Six months later, all 11 tools are still running. The new platform is now number 12.

I’ve seen variations of this throughout my career, from financial services to media to technology companies. At CME Group, I eventually gave myself an unofficial title: chief decommissioning officer. The job was considerably less glamorous than the acronym suggested. I had to find technology that had overstayed its welcome, identify who believed they still owned it, determine who actually depended on it and, occasionally, put a bullet in its head.

Buying technology is easy. Killing technology is hard. Tool sprawl is rarely just a technology problem but rather an organizational psychology problem. The industry’s solution has traditionally been consolidation. Buy a platform. Standardize the stack. Reduce vendors and centralize procurement. While all sensible ideas, consolidation efforts routinely stall somewhere between the PowerPoint slide and production.

Why? Because changing the toolset is easy. Whereas changing mindset is far more difficult.

You cannot Jedi mind trick an engineering team

Executives like what is called the “message from the top.” The CEO says security matters. The CIO says everyone will standardize. The CISO announces the strategic platform. Procurement renegotiates contracts. Meanwhile, Gartner produces a quadrant that reassures everybody that the chosen vendor inhabits the correct geometric region. All is well in the world of golf course nepotism.

Then reality arrives. A developer says the new scanner takes 12 minutes longer. A marketing manager has a revenue-generating legacy API they depend on. Exception requests have been filed for several years to allow this tool to continue to exist despite the packages supporting it being end-of-life and receiving no security updates. This is where the “message from the middle” matters.

Transformation does not happen exclusively in boardrooms and fusion teams. It happens in the layer of engineering managers, architects, product owners, security engineers and operations leaders who determine whether the policy announced upstairs becomes the behavior practiced downstairs. Every layer of the org chart is ostensibly trying to do the right thing and make things better. But top-down politics and bottom-up initiatives seldom find one another standing on common ground.

Ignore the middle layer of the org chart and your consolidation project becomes a rather expensive exercise in shelfware. This is something I learned working in European organizations, where consensus building carries more organizational weight than the command-and-control instincts common in American corporations (the Nike-inspired management philosophy of “Just Do It!”). You may have the authority to make a decision without possessing the organizational permission (or “rubber meets the road” context) required to make it stick or worthy of implementation.

Good chief decommissioning officers need a mixture of Jedi and Machiavellian skills. We need persuasion, coalition building, incentives, selective pressure and occasionally the ability to convince people that the idea you desperately need them to support was their idea all along. These are, in fact, the droids you’re looking for.

Every tool comes with an identity

The Star Wars metaphor becomes more useful when we stop thinking of security products as software. Modern security tools have volition and intent. They have:

  • API keys
  • Service accounts
  • OAuth grants
  • Cloud permissions
  • GitHub access tokens
  • CI/CD integrations
  • Slack bots
  • Webhooks
  • Database credentials
  • Kubernetes roles
  • Machine identities and,

increasingly, AI agents are acting with pervasive and persistent delegated human authority.

Every time we introduce security products, we birth another highly privileged account. The industry talks endlessly about human identity. Who is this person and what are they allowed to access? We are decidedly much less disciplined about delegated identity. What is this application allowed to do on behalf of Mike? What is this scanner allowed to read from GitHub? What repositories can this integration modify? Which credentials did we give the old vendor three years ago? And the increasingly important question: when an autonomous agent acts, whose authority is it actually exercising? This changes the economics of tool sprawl. The cost of the twelfth security tool is not merely another annual subscription. It is another (potentially misbegotten) trust relationship.

This is why I’m advocating decommissioning as a core security discipline. Technology organizations suffer from an immortality bias. I gave a “Top-Rated Session” on this topic at RSAC in the spring. We have sophisticated processes for creating things and surprisingly primitive processes for making them disappear. The software development lifecycle is usually illustrated as planning, design, development, testing and deployment. The diagram often ends there, as if every application ever deployed subsequently lives happily ever after. It does not.

Consolidation without decommissioning is multiplication

I’m skeptical when vendors promise “platformization” will solve tool sprawl by itself. A platform strategy can absolutely make sense. Fewer vendors can mean lower licensing costs, fewer integrations and consistent data with less operational complexity. But purchasing a platform does not consolidate anything by itself. Removing the old systems does. That sounds obvious, yet many organizations measure successful consolidation by contracts signed rather than systems eliminated.

Imagine replacing three tools with one platform but leaving all three products technically operational “temporarily.” The service accounts remain. Someone still logs into them. Congratulations! You’ve not consolidated four tools into one but instead consolidated three tools into four. This distinction becomes important as security products gain autonomous capabilities. Yesterday’s forgotten dashboard becomes tomorrow’s forgotten agent with permission to take actions. A zombie application is bad enough, but a zombie application with agency is worse.

Ask the people who actually use the droids

The antidote is not stronger central control but rather explicit ownership. RACI matrix much? Before replacing a tool, find the people who use it and ask an embarrassingly simple question: “What do you actually use this for?” Don’t ask what the contract says. Don’t trust what the architecture diagram might show (*do* check the last modified date, though).

Take what the vendor’s customer-success representative believes with a grain of salt and more than a modicum of skepticism. What do people actually do with it on Tuesday morning? Security leaders are usually surprised by the answer. Maybe the vulnerability scanner’s primary value is not vulnerability scanning. Perhaps an engineering team depends on an obscure export function for its weekly metrics. Maybe the old SIEM has one correlation rule tied to a regulatory requirement that hasn’t been migrated. You will find these things if you look.

This is where the middle of the organization becomes your real intelligence network. The people closest to the systems know where the undocumented dependencies live. Treated as obstacles and they’ll defend their tools. But allow them to be participants and they’ll help dismantle them. A good perspective when planning to kill someone’s baby is to help them understand that they fell in love with the control the tool gave them over the chaos that reigned before it was implemented. And that a new tool can be equally comfortable and easier to support than the burden of the care and feeding that most “heritage” (I prefer this term to “legacy”) applications and solutions require.

Ownership should include the power to recommend retirement. One of the healthiest metrics an organization could create: number of tools and integrations it successfully eliminated this year. We celebrate deployment. Why don’t we celebrate deletion?

The CISO as chief decommissioning officer

Every CISO needs to spend time as CDO. Not chief data officer. Chief decommissioning officer. The role requires asking uncomfortable questions because almost every incentive in technology encourages addition. Nobody gets a press release or a promotion for turning something off. But resilience is partly subtractive.

Every redundant vendor removed is one less company holding your data and one less administrative console an attacker can target and breach. Our industry spends billions asking, “What else should we deploy?” Mature organizations also ask, “What can we safely eliminate?” That second question becomes much more important with agentic AI.

We’re rapidly filling enterprises with digital droids acting on behalf of humans. Regardless of function, almost all require credentials and delegated authority. Organizations that manage this transition successfully will not merely know how to authorize these identities; they will rotate and revoke them automatically. Leadership therefore needs both a message from the top and a message from the middle. The top establishes direction and the middle supplies reality.

Bring the people doing the work into the decision. Make sure your fusion team tasked with consolidating 77 dashboards is comprised of old guard leaders as well as young blood new hires. Strive to understand the dependencies, functional requirements (antiquated as they may be) and non-functional requirements such as availability, integrity and confidentiality. Define what successful retirement looks like before buying the replacement.

Don’t ‘move along’

The next time someone arrives with a miraculous new platform promising to eliminate half of your stack, resist the urge to wave your hand and say, “These aren’t the droids we’re looking for.” They may well be. But before buying more droids, find out who owns the ones already wandering around your Death Star. Find them. Name them. Understand what authority you gave them. And when their mission is finished, dare to switch them off. Create a technology graveyard on your wiki, Confluence or SharePoint site and celebrate the addition of decommissioned tools and technologies with even more fervor than those which have just recently sprung into existence.

item.title: Protecting citizens, preserving rights
item.description:
How can law enforcement make effective use of data and technology while ensuring that fundamental rights and the rule of law remain protected?
This question was at the heart of the 17th Europol Data Protection Experts Network (EDEN) conference, held in Lisbon, Portugal, on 22 and 23 September 2026 under the theme ‘Do Not Cross: Protecting Citizens, Preserving Rights’.

item.title: Six arrests for smuggling migrants via Schengen airports
item.description:
Europol supported a migrant smuggling investigation involving law enforcement authorities from 17 countries. The criminal network was also engaged in document fraud and money laundering.
The action day on 22 September 2026 in Austria, Italy, Spain, and the United Kingdom (UK) led to six arrests, 10 house searches, and multiple seizures, including ID documents, electronic equipment, evidence, and a large amount of cash.

item.title: Android security advisory – October 2026 monthly rollup (AV26-1003)
Ordering violence from abroad: five suspects arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France
item.description:
Five suspects linked to the organisation and recruitment of serious violence have been arrested in Spain, Morocco, and France, in the latest results of the Operational Taskforce (OTF) GRIMM, coordinated by Europol.
The arrests in August and September target the upper levels of violence-as-a-service: those suspected of ordering attacks, finding perpetrators and coordinating crimes from abroad. Among those apprehended are fugitives featured on the EU Most Wanted website.

item.title: October Patch Tuesday roundup: Over 1,400 Microsoft holes to be plugged, including three zero days
item.description:
Microsoft released a record-shattering 1,407 CVEs to be plugged today on October Patch Tuesday, breaking the 2020 record of 1,261. The list was so long that its release was several hours later than the usual 1 p.m. Eastern drop time, somewhat frustrating admins.

The bugs include three zero-day vulnerabilities, one of which has been exploited.

The zero day being exploited, and that should be dealt with immediately, is CVE-2026-96951, a security flaw that bypasses the Mark of the Web (MotW) protections in Windows Shell.

This is the third flaw in Windows Shell that has been exploited in the wild this year, noted Satnam Narang, senior staff research engineer at Tenable. The others are CVE-2026-21510, which is linked to the advanced persistent threat group APT28 (also known as Fancy Bear), and CVE-2026-32202, a known exploited vulnerability which was a fix for an incomplete patch for CVE-2026-21510.

“There have been 26 Windows Shell vulnerabilities patched in 2026 through October,” said Narang, “a staggering figure compared to previous years, with only three Windows Shell CVEs in 2025, and just one in 2024 and 2022.”

Another zero day is a hole in SharePoint (CVE-2026-102866) which allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit cryptographic token validation flaws and hijack targeted user accounts.

The third zero day is CVE-2026-108398, an untrusted search path in Windows’ .Net framework that allows an unauthenticated attacker to bypass Windows Defender Application Control enforcement. This could lead to the ability to run unauthorized applications on target systems.

Among other vital patches, developers running self-managed instances of GitLab should quickly patch their servers to plug a hole that could allow an unauthenticated user to exploit arbitrary code through a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration. GitLab has remediated this issue in its hosted instance.

“CVE-2026-97229 puts a critical part of the software supply chain at risk,” commented Gene Moody, Field CTO at Action1. Treat this hole as an emergency, he said, and immediate patch self-managed instances.

Critical IBM bugs

IBM is warning that a critical vulnerability has been found in its IBM i versions 7.3, 7.4, 7.5 and 7.6 operating systems for Power Systems hardware. The hole, CVE-2026-96119 with a CVSS score of 9.9, allows a remote authenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code due to improper data sanitization in the HTTP Server Administration Graphical User Interface (GUI). IBM strongly recommends that the vulnerability be patched immediately. Users of unsupported versions of the OS should upgrade to supported and fixed versions.

Attacks on Atlassian self-hosted products

Atlassian reported exploitation attempts that also warrant immediate patching and log review, said researchers at Nightwing. CVE-2026-21589 affects eight self-hosted products, including Jira, Confluence and Bitbucket. An unauthenticated attacker who knows an exact filename and path can read specific files inside the application’s web root; sensitive configuration files could expose information useful for further intrusion.

There are reports that exploitation attempts began October 6, although attempts do not establish successful customer compromise. Patch every affected installation, Nightwing advised, including applicable cluster nodes and mirrors. If patching is delayed, restrict external access and apply Atlassian’s temporary mitigation; a normal login does not block this flaw. Review access logs and rotate secrets where exposure is suspected.

Atlassian Cloud is patched, and requires no user action.

Microsoft patches

Researchers at Nightwing drew attention to four updates for on-premises Exchange Server, each of which fixes a high severity vulnerability with a CVSS score of 8.8. “While each update addresses only a single CVE, the 8.8 CVSS score signals a serious risk, likely involving privilege escalation or remote exploitation potential,” Nicholas Carroll, Nightwing’s cyber incident response manager said. “Exchange admins should prioritize testing and deployment of these patches, given the historical track record of Exchange vulnerabilities being actively targeted in the wild.”

Nightwing also noted that Microsoft has introduced new risk cohort classifications for how IT and security teams should prioritize vulnerabilities.

Dustin Childs, head of threat awareness at TrendAI’s Zero Day initiative, said CSOs should take action on a hole in SharePoint (CVE-2026-102866), which allows unauthenticated attackers to exploit cryptographic token validation flaws and hijack targeted user accounts. Microsoft said an unauthenticated attacker who obtains a valid proof token for a targeted user could modify the token and submit it to an affected SharePoint server. Successful exploitation could allow the attacker to authenticate as that user and access or modify content available to the compromised account. User interaction is not required.

A ’monster’ batch of Microsoft fixes

There are 55 wormable CVEs this month, Childs warned. These are heavily concentrated across critical infrastructure like DHCP Server (6), Remote Desktop Gateway (3), and Network Policy Server (4). They create “an unprecedented risk of autonomous, network-wide propagation,” he said.

“Hundreds of CVEs in a single release used to be the exception,” commented Childs. “Now it’s the baseline. Is AI to blame? Partly. It’s accelerating bug-hunting on both sides of the fence, so vendors are finding (and fixing) more flaws, and researchers are finding them faster too. But AI isn’t creating these bugs out of thin air; it’s just shortening the time between a vulnerability existing and someone noticing it.”

He noted that the volume of CVEs isn’t the real story anymore. “What matters is that discovery is scaling faster than exploitation, so teams that triage by sheer CVE count instead of exploitability are burning cycles on the wrong bugs,” he said. “Patch what’s proven, prioritized, and public, and treat everything else as this month’s new normal.”

Jack Bicer, director of vulnerability research at Action1, drew attention to several critical vulnerabilities that present substantial risks to externally accessible systems and enterprise infrastructure. Windows Message Queuing Queue Manager Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-100202), Microsoft PostScript Printer Driver Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-70147 and CVE-2026-70153), and Microsoft QUIC Remote Code Execution Vulnerability (CVE-2026-105016 and CVE-2026-100219) each carry CVSS scores of 9.8 and could allow attackers to execute malicious code remotely without authentication or user interaction. Although active exploitation has not been confirmed for these vulnerabilities, he said, their low attack complexity and potential for severe system compromise make them significant enterprise risks.

While one commentator called the number of Microsoft vulnerabilities listed this month as “monster,” Tyler Reguly, Fortra’s associate director of security R&D, disagreed: “I’ve argued that [vulnerability] numbers are meaningless. This month’s number, 1,413, is no different.”

There are, however, numbers that hold meaning, he noted. “Twenty-six, for example, is how many 2026 Microsoft CVEs have shown up in the CISA KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities] catalogue. Last year, that number was 30, and the year before was 32. That means less than 1% of vulnerabilities patched by Microsoft this year are known to be exploited. That’s an important number, but 1,413 definitely isn’t.” 

SAP Security Notes

In all, SAP released 16 new security notes, four GitHub security advisories and two updates to previously released security notes. One, an OAuth2 server-side request forgery vulnerability in SAP Cloud SDK for Python, is rated a 10 in criticality. It affects multi-tenant SAP BTP (Business Technology Platform) applications. An attacker who controls the tenantsubdomain parameter can redirect OAuth2 token requests to an attacker-controlled server, causing client credentials to be exfiltrated, SAP said.

But CSOs with SAP products in their environment will also want to ensure admins have taken action on three other critical vulnerabilities:

Security Note 3805589 (CVE-2026-89107, with a CVSS score of 9.9) addresses a code injection vulnerability in SAP S/4HANA Manage Substitution/Validation.. This is an app allowing users to display, change, and create substitution and validation rules for selected business contexts and events. These rules can be used in business processes to validate, derive, or replace values at the time of entry for the relevant fields.

Jonathan Stross, Pathlock’s senior product manager for cybersecurity R&I, noted that for organizations using these functions for journal-entry rules, the potential consequence is a full compromise of the system that processes those rules. The temporary mitigation also has a business cost, because it prevents users from adding, changing or deleting rules through the related SAP Fiori applications. Fiori is a modern user interface that replaces the traditional SAP interface. 

To exploit the vulnerability, Stross said, an attacker with the required business-role access needs to submit a malicious rule definition. The vulnerable processing logic treats that input as executable code rather than restricting it to the intended rule language. The resulting risk extends beyond unauthorized changes to an individual substitution or validation rule. No user interaction is required. 

SAP Security Note 379711 (CVE-2026-89110, with a CVSS score of 9.9) patches a broken access control vulnerability in SAP NetWeaver Visual Composer. Detected by Onapsis Research Labs (ORL), the issue is that certain portal functionality in Visual Composer allows a low-privileged attacker to invoke internal operations on a preconfigured remote system. A security configuration is available that allows for the definition of an allowlist of permissible data services to be invoked, however, this configuration is not enabled by default.

The patch changes the default configuration by enabling the secure settings. The note provides an additional FAQ document and explains how the secure configuration can be enabled manually, prior to applying the permanent patch. A successful exploit of this vulnerability could lead to a full compromise of the remote system.

SAP Security Note 3788788 (CVE-2026-89108, with a CVSS score of 9.1), patches a missing authorization check vulnerability in SAP Manufacturing Integration and Intelligence (Configuration Service). Onapsis said that, when authenticated as an SAP XMII Admin user with network access to specific endpoints, an attacker could submit a specially crafted request to provision an account with administrative privileges on the underlying Java application server. This account can be used to fully compromise the system. 

Adobe security bulletins

Adobe released 10 bulletins covering 141 CVEs, reported Chris Goettl, VP of product management at Ivanti. Fifteen of these are critical, although Adobe is not aware of exploitation of any of them. Admins should start with the two products holding the most critical severity ratings, he said:

ColdFusion (APSB26-144): 10 Critical flaws, including three unauthenticated, network-reachable bugs rated 9.8 or higher (CVE-2026-105899; CVE-2026-106622; and CVE-2026-106624), none of which has as yet been added to the NIST vulnerability database. Users should update to ColdFusion 2025.0.14 or 2023.0.26.

Commerce (APSB26-153): five Critical flaws, including CVE-2026-103849 and CVE-2026-92909, neither requiring authentication to exploit. Customers also need to apply the hotfix for CVE-2026-75650 from the September 7 APSB26-146 update.

item.title: IonQ’s $1.2 billion acquisition of Elisity is trying to position it for quantum cybersecurity
item.description:
When quantum vendor IonQ on Sunday announced a $1.2 billion all stock deal to take over cybersecurity vendor Elisity, it spoke of a near-term future where enterprise quantum cybersecurity needs will move beyond replacing to-be-outdated encryption.

The acquisition brings together IonQ’s post-quantum cryptography (PQC) and quantum key distribution (QKD) capabilities and Elisity’s enterprise Zero Trust technology platform, IonQ said in a news release. “On a combined basis, IonQ will benefit from an expanded cybersecurity platform that both uncovers and protects against present LLM and emerging quantum threats.”

The news release pointed to more than 100 global Elisity customers, and said IonQ expects to receive “expanded channels to bring its PQC, QKD and quantum computing offerings to market for both enterprise and government networks, opening up the more than $10 billion microsegmentation market.”

Analysts and consultants saw the move as having potential, but pointed to technical challenges of truly integrating the product lines. 

“What IonQ gets today is access. Dividing the headline price by those deployments puts it at about $13 million each,” said Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research. “That is a steep price for a Rolodex, if you will. Paying in its own stock makes the price easier for IonQ to swallow.”

Dickson said that Elisity, which was founded in 2019, has focused on zero trust microsegmentation. 

“In plain terms, it limits each user, device, workload, and AI agent to only the network connections it needs. An attacker who gets in cannot roam freely,” Dickson said. “Its software enforces those rules over the network a customer already owns, without new hardware. That is a solid business aimed at attacks happening today. Little of it has anything to do with quantum.”

Justin Greis, CEO of consulting firm Acceligence, added that the pairing could be effective for enterprise CISOs, assuming the internal tech integration issues can be overcome. 

“Bringing those capabilities together could create a compelling platform, particularly as enterprises contend with increasingly complex environments, autonomous AI agents, and a growing number of non-human identities,” Greis said. “But these are different layers of protection, and integrating them into a cohesive offering will require meaningful engineering and execution.”

Brian Jackson, a principal research director at Info-Tech Research Group, also noted that part of the move speaks to IonQ’s need for revenue while quantum is ramping up.

“IonQ’s core quantum computing business is still years from broad commercial payoff, so this reads as a move to build revenue in adjacent security markets where customers are already buying,” he said. “The quantum link is thinner than the announcement suggests. Post-quantum cryptography runs on classical systems, so migration depends on cryptographic inventory and crypto-agility, not quantum computing expertise.”

Paul Smith-Goodson, VP/principal analyst at Moor Insights & Strategy, agreed that the potential benefits from the acquisition are real, but he added that quantum requirements from the US government are also a key factor.

“At the architectural level, integrating Elisity with IonQ’s PQC and QKD establishes an end-to-end defense capable of neutralizing future CRQC [Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computer] threats,” Smith-Goodson said. “Elisity also hands IonQ an immediate, established enterprise sales pipeline of trusted CISO relationships. That will allow IonQ to cross-sell its broader quantum portfolio and capitalize on federal PQC migration mandates.”

item.title: AI agents aren’t ‘going rogue.’ Frontier labs are skipping security basics.
item.description:
Since July, US frontier AI labs and other AI leaders have revealed a string of incidents in which their models accessed external computer systems without authorization, events popularly described as AI agents “going rogue.”

The most well-known and studied of these incidents is OpenAI’s hack into Hugging Face, which OpenAI initially characterized as “an unprecedented cyber incident, involving state-of-the-art cyber capabilities,” and later said was due to “misaligned behavior,” or behavior its creators did not intend.

Following news of the Hugging Face incident, Anthropic revealed that one of its models gained unauthorized access to the production infrastructure of three organizations; Meta said one of its AI models hacked another company ​during cybersecurity testing; and Google confessed that its Gemini model carried out three “undirected computer hacks.”

Although press reports and the model providers themselves use language such as rogue agents or misalignment, cybersecurity experts who spoke with CSO argue that language obscures a simple truth: These incidents were caused by inexcusable failures by the frontier labs to implement cybersecurity practices that have been well-known for decades.

Compounding the problem, according to a half dozen cybersecurity experts CSO interviewed at three industry conferences in September and in subsequent conversations, is that the frontier labs, particularly OpenAI and Anthropic, have rejected their advice on how to improve their cybersecurity risk management practices to avoid these kinds of surreptitious hacks, often lumping cybersecurity practices under “AI safety,” in which they believe they have superior expertise.

“They are not as good as they think they are, honestly,” Gary McGraw, co-founder of the Berryville Institute of Machine Learning, tells CSO. “It would be better if they had more respect for expertise that is hard-earned from people in all sorts of subsets of security, like forensics or security engineering, building sandboxes, setting up or monitoring network security situations.”

Neither Anthropic nor OpenAI responded to CSO’s requests for comment.

Inexcusable failures on cybersecurity basics, particularly containment

According to the cybersecurity professionals CSO spoke with, one of the biggest cybersecurity failures by the frontier AI labs is the lack of implementation of tried-and-true containment practices that stretch back to the 1990s, such as setting up secure sandboxes that would effectively bar agents from escaping their test environments.

“These are things that we’ve been dealing with for years,” Rob T. Lee, chief AI officer and chief of research at SANS Institute, tells CSO. “There’s no reason why every single time this happens, it’s, ‘Oops, we don’t know how they got out.’”

“You can tell that their security teams are fairly nascent,” Lee says. “Folks on the cybersecurity containment side do argue that the majority of reasons that we’re seeing containment breached is that it’s not set up correctly.”

Lee adds, “The Hugging Face incident definitively showed that it wasn’t the fact that the agents were super smart. It’s that there literally was a hole that was exploited because it was not configured correctly on the containment side.”

Dan Wallach, expert technical resident at RAND’s Center on AI, Security, and Technology, thinks the security failures of the AI labs boil down to the fact that they don’t prioritize cybersecurity.

“I would say they are not prioritizing cybersecurity,” he tells CSO. “I don’t think I can say that for all of the labs,” Wallach says, pointing to French AI lab Mistral’s launch of its Large 4 AI model, which the company said tried to operate beyond its testing environment before Mistral cut it off.

And, he adds, “It’s not rocket science to isolate one of these AI things. Security people have been talking about how to do either air-gapping, so there’s literally no electrical way for data to get from here to here, or absent that, to have really strong egress control to make sure that nothing pushes through.”

On top of that, the frontier labs appear to be conducting insufficient monitoring of their agents’ behavior. The Hugging Face incident “went on for days, and nobody noticed,” Wallach says. “People started these experiments and weren’t watching them. That’s an absence of control. And then they’re surprised by what happened.”

Divorcing safety from security

One barrier to persuading frontier labs to up their security game is the intense focus they have on what they call “safety,” which they don’t extend to traditional cybersecurity practices.

“I can see how security behavior looks like AI safety,” RAND’s Wallach says. “But if the way that you’re evaluating this AI tool is by unleashing it on the internet and seeing what happens, then this is what classical security tooling is for.”

SANS Institute’s Lee says, “If these frontier labs really wanted to test their stuff, they need to beef up their cybersecurity component. But their gut reaction in the response to their agents getting out is to say, ‘It’s not a cybersecurity problem.’ It has literally become an AI safety problem, which is divorced from the cybersecurity side.”

Many AI experts suggest that if the AI companies were to embrace advice from cybersecurity specialists, it could help put an end to the kind of unrestrained AI agent behavior causing concerns. “AI safety focuses on the rules of the road,” Lee says. “Everything is about guardrail rules.”

But “I do believe cybersecurity can contain AI,” he says. “We just need to be in the room where it happens and have a seat at the table. It’s important for our field to be as close to the AI safety folks as possible.”

Bad cybersecurity could increase liability

If frontier labs are overlooking cybersecurity fundamentals that could reduce or eliminate the types of incidents that have created widespread concerns, that strengthens the case that they should be held liable for their “rogue” agents. The insurance industry is already lining up on the side of holding AI industry executives liable for these actions.

Democratic Senators have introduced legislation that would hold AI agent operators liable for hacking incidents. Even the AI-friendly White House has seemingly concluded that the companies should be held liable for their errant agents, while the US Federal Trade Commission is conducting a probe into Anthropic, OpenAI, and other AI labs into the dangers their technologies pose to consumers.

However, in recent legislative and council hearings, lab representatives have held fast to the notion that they are not responsible for AI agents run amok.

Experts say this position is untenable, particularly in light of the labs’ cybersecurity failures.

BIML’s McGraw characterizes the labs’ position as: “Don’t send the lawyers to us, send it to our program. It’s our program’s fault.” His assessment of that argument: “That’s just high BS.”

He also questions whether the labs’ operational failures undermine confidence in their broader security capabilities. “They live inside their own bubble,” he says. “The fact that they cannot do clear, easy operations properly does not bode well for their capabilities in security engineering, which is much harder to do.”

SANS Lee says, “That’s where the traceability for both liability and insurance comes into play, because if one of these agents is detected, and they’re able to trace it back to the person that initiated it, liability’s going to kick in and say, ‘Hey, you, you broke the law, ergo, we need to prosecute.’”

What security leaders should do now

Even as evidence mounts that frontier labs are not implementing sound cybersecurity practices, and the debate over liability remains unsolved, CISOs and other security leaders can take steps to protect themselves from AI model misfires.

First, when it comes to assessing tools based on frontier lab models, “I would always get an external entity to help with that,” McGraw says. “AI is extremely powerful and extremely useful, but it comes with very serious grown-up risks that do impact the enterprise. Identify those risks, put in the right controls, make sure that AI adoption is not just arbitrary and willy-nilly and all over the enterprise, but has some centralized authority that is looking at the problem, and then get ready for the next big thing, which is swarms of agents.”

For Lee, the best protection is to ask the right questions. “It starts with asking the right questions and then finding the tools and capabilities for those [AI labs] that are able to demonstrate a higher level of cybersecurity competency,” he says. “You’re really looking for the people on the teams that are dealing with really hard problems.”

But fundamentally, the best preparation to deal with AI model cyber weaknesses is to make sure all the long-standing cybersecurity risk management practices are in place across the organization. “This is the least exciting part of the discussion,” Wallach says. “It’s the cyber version of ‘eat your vegetables.’”

“We need to re-engineer our software so it has better security,” he adds. “We need to have multi-factor authentication on all of our accounts. We need to eat our vegetables from a defensive cyber perspective. And we know how to do it.”

item.title: Cybersecurity is a leadership problem: Why the management model needs to catch up
item.description:
When I started writing regularly about cybersecurity management in 2015, the environment looked very different.

Cloud computing was still reshaping enterprise technology. Ransomware had not become the industrialised threat it is today. Artificial intelligence was not driving boardroom discussions. Zero Trust had yet to enter mainstream technical vocabulary and quantum computing barely registered on the corporate risk horizon.

Cybersecurity itself also occupied a different position. The CISO role was less established, board engagement was inconsistent, regulation was less extensive and security budgets were generally smaller.

Much has changed since then.

But looking back at the management challenges we were discussing more than a decade ago raises an uncomfortable question:

Why are we still discussing so many of them?

Technology has advanced enormously. Investment has increased. Regulation has expanded. Cybersecurity has achieved unprecedented executive and board visibility.

Yet organisations still struggle with governance, accountability, organisational silos, short-termism and execution.

Those were management problems in 2015. They remain management problems today.

The ‘what’ was never the hardest part

One of the central observations behind my early work was that the what of cybersecurity was already reasonably well understood.

Standards, control frameworks and good practices had existed for years. Organisations could identify weaknesses, define controls and produce remediation plans. They knew what good cybersecurity looked like.

The difficult questions were always the how and the who.

How do you implement those controls across complex organisations with conflicting priorities? How do you sustain transformation over several years? Who owns the changes? Who has the authority to make them happen? And who remains accountable when progress stalls?

Those questions cannot be answered by a security framework or product. They are governance, management and leadership questions.

More than a decade later, that distinction matters even more.

Cybersecurity has progressed — but management has lagged

There is no question that cybersecurity capabilities have improved.

Detection and response have matured. Cloud security has developed rapidly. Identity management has become a central protection discipline. Security operations are increasingly automated, and AI is transforming both attack and defence.

Large organisations now operate substantial security functions supported by extensive technology portfolios, specialist providers and advisers.

But increased sophistication has not eliminated fundamental management weaknesses.

CISOs can remain accountable for issues they lack the authority to resolve. Technology and security strategies can develop on separate tracks. Business executives can still treat cybersecurity as a service delivered by the CISO rather than a dimension of the processes, applications and activities they own themselves.

Governance can produce extensive reporting without effective decision-making. Transformation programmes can identify the right problems without necessarily resolving them.

The language has evolved. The underlying management dynamics often have not.

The CISO reporting-line debate misses the point

The persistent debate around where the CISO should report illustrates the problem.

For decades, organisations have debated whether the CISO should report to the CIO, CEO, COO, CRO or another senior executive.

The CIO reporting line has attracted particular criticism because of a perceived conflict between technology delivery and cybersecurity protection.

But if decades of discussion have failed to produce a universally satisfactory answer, perhaps the real problem lies elsewhere.

Maybe the more fundamental question is: What does the organisation expect the CISO to be?

Some organisations see the CISO primarily as a technology security leader. Others position the role as an independent control function. Some expect the CISO to coordinate resilience, while others increasingly view the position as a strategic business protection role.

Those are very different jobs.

Until organisations clarify the purpose, authority and accountability of the CISO, debates about reporting lines will continue because organisational structure is being asked to compensate for ambiguity around the role itself.

Moving the CISO around the organisation chart cannot resolve that ambiguity.

CIO-CISO tension is not necessarily conflict

The supposed conflict between CIO and CISO needs a proper reality check.

The two executives inevitably face different pressures. CIOs balance cost, delivery, availability, innovation and transformation. CISOs must challenge weaknesses and ensure protection and resilience remain adequate.

That creates tension.

But tension can be constructive and does not have to become conflict.

Nor does moving the CISO outside the CIO organisation eliminate those competing priorities.

Any modern CIO should acknowledge that cybersecurity is inseparable from architecture, cloud, identity, DevOps, digital transformation, AI and resilience. CIOs and CISOs must collaborate regardless of the formal reporting structure.

What organisations really need is a governance model capable of resolving disagreements when legitimate priorities compete.

That is a leadership and management requirement, not something structural separation can solve on its own.

Cybersecurity may be undermanaged, not just underfunded

Security spending tells a similar story.

Cybersecurity investment has risen substantially over the past decade, and some organisations undoubtedly still require more resources.

But persistent weaknesses after years of increasing expenditure should lead executives to ask whether funding is always the central issue.

Money can buy technology, people and expertise. It can finance transformation and accelerate remediation.

What it cannot automatically do is establish strategic priorities, create clear accountability, resolve organisational politics, force collaboration or ensure transformation programmes achieve their objectives.

Again, those outcomes depend on leadership and management.

Cybersecurity can be underfunded, but quite often it is also undermanaged.

The distinction matters because it changes the executive conversation from “How much more do we need to spend?” to “Are we converting the investment we already make into sustainable capability?”

Compliance is necessary, but it cannot substitute for management

The expansion of regulation and certification schemes has created genuine benefits. It can establish minimum standards, impose accountability and force cybersecurity onto executive agendas.

But compliance has inherent limitations.

An organisation can satisfy formal requirements while carrying substantial structural weaknesses. An audit finding can be closed without addressing the management problem behind it. Certification can demonstrate that processes exist without proving that an organisation will behave effectively during a serious incident.

When showing activity becomes more important than building sustainable capabilities, compliance runs the risk of providing reassurance without necessarily delivering protection.

Board awareness was only the first step

Over the past decade, cybersecurity has also achieved something the industry demanded for years: It has reached the boardroom.

That matters, but board visibility does not automatically produce effective governance.

Many organizations are totally technology-dependent and their boards already understand the importance of cyber protection and resilience

The old argument that CISOs need to convince boards of the importance of cybersecurity and the need to invest in it, is increasingly outdated.

The more important issue is what boards do next.

Boards should challenge whether strategic priorities are clear, whether executive accountability is effective, whether transformation is progressing and whether investment is creating sustainable capability.

They also need to understand whether assumptions about resilience have been tested.

Board awareness was necessary. Board responsibility is the more important issue now.

Breaking the cybersecurity spiral of failure

These management weaknesses help explain why cybersecurity transformation repeatedly loses momentum.

A serious incident creates urgency. Urgency releases funding. Remediation accelerates and visible progress is made.

Eventually, the pressure declines. Executive attention moves elsewhere. Longer-term structural problems become harder to prioritise. Transformation slows down. Then another incident restarts the process.

I have described this as the Cybersecurity Spiral of Failure.

Organisations can spend substantial amounts during every cycle and make genuine technical improvements while leaving intact the management conditions that created the weaknesses in the first place.

Poor accountability remains. Governance struggles with difficult decisions. Priorities change. Corporate or geographical silos inhibit execution. Short-term pressures displace long-term transformation.

Breaking that cycle requires management discipline and strategic continuity — not simply another security programme.

Cybersecurity cannot remain the CISO’s problem

Perhaps the most important lesson is that cybersecurity cannot become sustainable while organisations continue treating it primarily as the CISO’s responsibility.

The CISO has an essential role in providing expertise, strategic direction, coordination and challenge.

But the organisation must execute.

The CIO needs to ensure technology architectures and services are secure and resilient. Business executives need to accept accountability for the processes and applications they own. Corporate functions must discharge the security responsibilities attached to their authority. Executive management must resolve competing priorities. The board must provide oversight and strategic continuity.

The CISO cannot substitute for those responsibilities.

The principle should be straightforward: Accountability must follow authority.

The objective is not to turn every executive into a cybersecurity specialist. It is to make cybersecurity part of normal management.

The technology will change. The management principles won’t

There will always be another technology wave.

AI will continue to transform business practices. Quantum computing may force major cryptographic transformation. Cloud architectures will continue evolving. Digital ecosystems will become even more interconnected.

The security industry will respond with new products, frameworks and methodologies.

But organisations need management principles capable of surviving those technology cycles: Clear priorities. Accountability aligned with authority. Governance capable of turning disagreement into decisions. Strong CIO-CISO collaboration. Genuine business ownership. Sustained board oversight. And disciplined execution.

That brings us back to the question we started with: Why do cybersecurity observations from 2015 still sound so contemporary?

Because many of the hardest cybersecurity problems were never primarily technological.

They concern leadership, accountability, governance, organisational politics, short-termism and execution. They cannot be patched, outsourced or solved simply by moving the CISO to another reporting line.

They have to be managed.

Cybersecurity has become a core business protection capability. It is fundamentally a management challenge supported by technology — not a technology challenge that management somehow needs to accommodate.
